issues.legal_issue: A de facto guardian who is not the minor’s legal guardian cannot bind the minor’s immovable property through a settlement, and describing the transaction as a family arrangement does not validate it.
material_facts: A minor heir’s elder brother executed a deed distributing estate property on the minor’s behalf.
The brother was not the minor’s legal guardian and had no authority to transfer the minor’s interest in immovable property.
The deed was defended as a family settlement and was found by the trial court to be beneficial to the minor.
The deed was held void, not only as to the minor but as to all parties to it.
issues.conclusion: The deed could not bind the minor, and its invalidity meant it was void as to all parties, including those who were legally competent.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mahomedan law, a de facto guardian has no power to convey to another an interest in a minor’s immovable property that the transferee can enforce against the minor; whether the transaction benefits the minor is immaterial. A void transaction cannot be made valid merely by describing it as a family arrangement. The Court relied on Imambandi v. Mutsaddi (1918) 45 I.A. 73 and rejected the contrary reasoning in Mahomed Keramutullah Miah v. Keramatulla, A.I.R. 1919 Cal. 218, and Ameer Hassan v. Md. Ejaz Hussain, A.I.R. 1929 Oudh 134.

predicates.minor_heir_property_settlement_dispute: The dispute concerns a settlement of estate property that purports to affect a minor heir’s interest.
predicates.minor_interest_in_immovable_property_tra: The settlement purports to transfer or distribute the minor’s interest in immovable property.
predicates.representative_not_legal_guardian: The person acting for the minor is not the minor’s legal guardian.

issues.definition: When a settlement dispute concerns a minor’s immovable property and the purported representative is not the minor’s legal guardian, the settlement is void as to all parties.

issues.legal_issue: Prolonged and continuous cohabitation as spouses, in the absence of an insurmountable obstacle to marriage, gives rise to a presumption of lawful marriage and supports the legitimacy of children born of the union.
material_facts: The woman and the deceased lived openly together as husband and wife for 23 to 24 years, and children were born to them.
Their children and the woman lived in the family home, and relatives and friends treated them as a family.
A property sale deed described two of the children as the deceased’s sons, and the settlement deed described the woman as his widow and the children as his children.
The evidence that the woman had been married to another man who was still alive was disbelieved, and no insurmountable obstacle to marriage was established.
issues.conclusion: The presumption of lawful marriage arose; the woman was the deceased’s lawfully wedded wife and the children born of the union were legitimate.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mahomedan law, prolonged and continuous cohabitation as husband and wife, where there is no insurmountable obstacle to marriage, supports a presumption that a lawful marriage took place. The presumption does not arise from mere casual concubinage or where an insurmountable obstacle exists, and may not apply where the parties’ conduct is incompatible with marriage. The Court relied on Khaja Hidayut Oollah v. Rai Jan Khanam (1844) 3 Moore’s Indian Appeals 295 and referred to the Privy Council decisions reported at 21 Indian Appeals 56 and 37 Indian Appeals 105, as well as Mulla’s Mahomedan Law, section 268.

predicates.marital_status_inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over marital status and the legitimacy of children in an inheritance claim.
predicates.prolonged_continuous_cohabitation_as_spo: A man and woman cohabit continuously for a prolonged period and are treated as spouses.
predicates.insurmountable_obstacle_to_marriage: An obstacle exists that makes marriage between the man and woman impossible.

issues.definition: In a marital-status inheritance dispute, prolonged continuous cohabitation as spouses without an insurmountable obstacle supports a presumption of lawful marriage and legitimacy.

issues.legal_issue: Mesne profits cannot be awarded when the plaint does not claim them, and a general prayer for possession and the rights attached to property does not include that claim.
material_facts: The plaint sought possession and the rights appertaining to the property but did not claim mesne profits.
The High Court included mesne profits in its decree.
The Supreme Court held that the general wording of the possession claim did not encompass mesne profits and deleted that part of the decree.
issues.conclusion: The award of mesne profits was erroneous and was deleted from the decree.
issues.legal_principle: A court cannot award mesne profits when they were not claimed in the plaint; a general claim for possession and rights appertaining to the property does not amount to such a claim. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_challenges_decree_awarding_mesne_: An appeal challenges a decree that awards mesne profits.
predicates.possession_claim_in_plaint: The plaint seeks possession of property and the rights attached to it.
predicates.mesne_profits_claimed_in_plaint: The plaint expressly claims mesne profits.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an award of mesne profits in a suit seeking possession, the award is not sustainable if the plaint did not claim mesne profits.
